Submission received: 11 January 2023 / Revised: 20 February 2023 / Accepted: 2 March 2023 / Published: 6 March 2023 Abstract Prognostic analysis for patient survival often employs gene expressions obtained from high-throughput screening for tumor tissues from patients. When dealing with survival data, a dependent censoring phenomenon arises, and thus the traditional Cox model may not correctly identify the effect of each gene. A copula-based gene selection model can effectively adjust for dependent censoring, yielding a multi-gene predictor for survival prognosis. However, methods to assess the impact of various types of dependent censoring on the multi-gene predictor have not been developed. In this article, we propose a sensitivity analysis method using the copula-graphic estimator under dependent censoring, and implement relevant methods in the R package “compound.Cox”. The purpose of the proposed method is to investigate the sensitivity of the multi-gene predictor to a variety of dependent censoring mechanisms. In order to make the proposed sensitivity analysis practical, we develop a web application. We apply the proposed method and the web application to a lung cancer dataset. We provide a template file so that developers can modify the template to establish their own web applications. 1. Introduction Prognostic analysis for survival often employs gene expressions obtained from high-throughput screening for tumor tissues from patients [1,2,3,4,5,6]. Here, the primary interest is often to find a set of genes that are strong predictors of survival. The simplest and yet most commonly used approach is to select a small number of significant genes found in a sequence of univariate Cox models fitted to patients’ survival data [5,6,7,8,9]. A linear predictor using multiple genes has been shown to be useful for survival prediction. Usually, a multi-gene predictor is more accurate than a single-gene predictor as the prognostic ability of a single gene is limited. A predictor optimally constructed from the selected genes becomes a useful biomarker for predicting survival in breast cancer [10,11,12,13,14,15], lung cancer [6,7,8,9,16,17], gastric cancer [18,19], ovarian cancer [20,21,22,23,24], skin cancer [25], liver cancer [26,27], bladder cancer [28], head and neck cancer [29,30], glioma [31], myeloproliferative neoplasms [32], kidney cancer [33], and cancers of mixed types [34,35]. These analyses were performed mostly based on univariate Cox regression with the significance scaling of p-values, such as 0.05, 0.01, and 0.001, followed by cross-validation and/or external validation. The primary reason for applying Cox regression is that it can easily handle censored survival times, i.e., survival time may not be observable for all patients under investigation. However, Cox regression critically relies on the independent censoring assumption: survival time and censoring time need to be statistically independent. This assumption is easily violated when patients drop out from the study due to the worsening of his/her health condition or patients are removed for transplantation [36,37]. Dependent censoring also arises due to unobserved factor [38,39,40,41]. In such cases, survival time is censored dependently on their health status. If the independent censoring assumption is violated, Cox regression analyses may not correctly identify the effect of each gene and thus may fail to select truly effective genes [41]. Therefore, the resultant predictor based on selected genes may have reduced ability to predict survival. A copula-based gene selection approach [41] can effectively adjust for dependent censoring, yielding a multi-gene predictor. Besides the development of a multi-gene predictor, copula-based dependent censoring models have gained popularity in recent years for dealing with survival data [42,43,44,45,46,47,48,49,50]. However, methods to assess the impact of various types of dependent censoring on the multi-gene predictor have not been developed. In this article, we propose a sensitivity analysis method using the copula-graphic estimator [47,51,52,53,54,55,56] under dependent censoring, and implement relevant methods in the R package compound.Cox [9]. This article aims to fill this gap by proposing detailed statistical methodologies; see Section 3 for details. Another important goal of this article is to establish a Shiny-based web application (in Section 4) that can be manipulated by any user online without installing any software. This effectively connects the development of a sensitivity analysis and its implementation in order to carry out a patient’s prognosis. The application is written by R packages Shiny [57] and compound.Cox [9]. While this application is developed using data on lung cancer patients, the computational framework can be extended to other survival data from other patients. We provide the R code in Supplementary Materials so that users can easily edit the code to be adapted to their own data analyses. fetched_contents.text: Recurrence of Papillary Thyroid Cancer: A Systematic Appraisal of Risk Factors Abstract Context Thyroid cancer recurrence is associated with increased mortality and adverse outcomes. Recurrence risk is currently predicted using clinical tools, often restaging patients after treatment. Detailed understanding of recurrence risk at disease onset could lead to personalized and improved patient care. Objective We aimed to perform a comprehensive bioinformatic and experimental analysis of 3 levels of genetic change (mRNA, microRNA, and somatic mutation) apparent in recurrent tumors and construct a new combinatorial prognostic risk model. Methods We analyzed The Cancer Genome Atlas data (TCGA) to identify differentially expressed genes (mRNA/microRNA) in 46 recurrent vs 455 nonrecurrent thyroid tumors. Two exonic mutational pipelines were used to identify somatic mutations. Functional gene analysis was performed in cell-based assays in multiple thyroid cell lines. The prognostic value of genes was evaluated with TCGA datasets. Results We identified 128 new potential biomarkers associated with recurrence, including 40 mRNAs, 39 miRNAs, and 59 genetic variants. Among differentially expressed genes, modulation of FN1, ITGα3, and MET had a significant impact on thyroid cancer cell migration. Similarly, ablation of miR-486 and miR-1179 significantly increased migration of TPC-1 and SW1736 cells. We further utilized genes with a validated functional role and identified a 5-gene risk score classifier as an independent predictor of thyroid cancer recurrence. Conclusion Our newly proposed risk model based on combinatorial mRNA and microRNA expression has potential clinical utility as a prognostic indicator of recurrence. These findings should facilitate earlier prediction of recurrence with implications for improving patient outcome by tailoring treatment to disease risk and increasing posttreatment surveillance. Keywords: papillary, thyroid, recurrence, miRNA, TCGA ---------------------------------------- Thyroid cancer recurrence is associated with increased mortality (1, 2), and early detection of thyroid cancer recurrence has been shown to improve patient outcomes (3, 4). Currently, risk of recurrence is predicted using clinical tools that often restage patients after their cancer treatment. While this is useful in stratifying patients to the level of follow-up and degree of thyrotropin (thyroid stimulating hormone) suppression required postoperatively, it does not inform the surgeon and patient about risk of recurrence until after all treatment has been completed. The primary management of thyroid neck recurrence remains surgical, with any microscopic residual disease managed via radioiodine if the malignancy is radioiodine avid (5). Distant metastases of differentiated thyroid cancer are often not radioiodine avid (4) and are particularly difficult to treat. If not amenable to surgery, radioiodine refractory disease can be considered for high-dose external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) (6), but this is considered much less effective. Sometimes radioresistant disease can be indolent and can be monitored (5). For rapidly progressive, symptomatic, or imminently threatening disease not amenable to local control, kinase inhibitor therapy can be considered (5), although this has a significant associated morbidity. Despite recent progress, most patients’ tumors eventually stop responding to kinase inhibitor therapies, and almost all patients have adverse events (7-10). Therapy targeted to individual patient genotype and phenotype may be key to future progress (11). Within this broader context, understanding which thyroid carcinomas are going to recur, and the functional reasons behind the recurrence, will be crucial to improving patient care. For a malignancy to recur, the primary disease must evade treatment. Tumor cell dormancy has been postulated as a means by which cancer cells achieve this (12). The most common site of recurrence is the cervical lymph nodes (13), and metastatic dormancy may be a key component of how cancer cells survive but do not progress immediately in a metastatic environment (14). The identification of cancer cells in adequately treated patients lends support to the dormancy theory and could contribute to explaining how some thyroid cancer patients have a recurrence many years after their primary disease (15). An important concept then, is how dormant cancer cells “activate” to cause such recurrence. There are multiple accompanying mechanisms which may contribute to thyroid cancer recurrence, including increased angiogenesis (16), escape from immune detection (17), and changes in the extracellular matrix (15). Investigating alterations in such pathways to identify significant biomarkers of thyroid cancer recurrence is important due to the significant morbidity and mortality associated with recurrence. Here, analysis of existing next-generation sequencing data was employed to investigate gene (mRNA/microRNA [miR]) expression changes and somatic mutational profiles associated with thyroid cancer recurrence. By performing in vitro investigations to determine the functional impact of these biomarkers, we aimed to discover how they might relate to the clinical outcome of thyroid cancer patients. Published in final edited form as: Best Pract Res Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2016 Nov 1;30(5):603–619. doi: 10.1016/j.beem.2016.10.001 Abstract The microRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNA comprising approximately 19–25 nucleotides. miRNAs can act as tumour suppressors or oncogenes, and aberrant expression of miRNAs has been reported in several human cancers and has been associated with cancer initiation and progression. Recent evidence suggests that miRNAs play a major role in thyroid carcinogenesis. In this review, we summarize the role of miRNAs in thyroid cancer and describe the oncogenic or tumour suppressor function of miRNAs as well as their clinical utility as prognostic or diagnostic markers in thyroid cancer. Keywords: microRNA, thyroid cancer, diagnosis, prognosis, treatment, circulating microRNA Introduction MicroRNAs (miRNA) are small non-coding RNAs that are approximately 19–25 nucleotides in length. The miRNAs regulate gene expression at the posttranscriptional level in both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells. The discovery of miRNA has opened new insights into the biological processes leading to cancer initiation and progression. Although most miRNAs target the 3′ untranslated region of the mRNA targets, some miRNA can also interact with the coding sequence of the target gene. A single miRNA can bind to a large number of different gene mRNAs. Thus, miRNA regulation of mRNA plays a major role in several biological functions in normal and pathological conditions [1]. Although the expression of miRNAs is tightly regulated, cancer initiation and progression have been associated with dysregulated miRNA expression [2–6]. In several cancers, miRNAs have been shown to be good diagnostic and prognostic markers. Studies have also shown that the aberrant expression of miRNAs plays an important role in cancer cell proliferation, differentiation, invasion, migration and cell death. Biological plausibility of upregulated miRNAs for thyroid cancer recurrence

The evidence strongly supports that upregulated miRNAs are implicated in thyroid cancer progression, but the biological plausibility for recurrence specifically is more nuanced than for general survival. The reviewed material identifies miR-221, miR-222, miR-146a, miR-181a, and miR-200c as miRNAs associated with thyroid cancer biology, with miR-221 and miR-222 most prominently linked to tumor suppression and cell-cycle regulation [N4-R1][N4-F2]. In thyroid cancer, miR-221 and miR-222 are described as direct regulators of p27, a tumor suppressor and cell-cycle regulator, and their overexpression is associated with reduced p27 expression and with aggressive disease behavior, advanced disease stage, extrathyroidal invasion, and lymph node metastasis [N4-R1][N4-F2]. This is important because progression-associated changes in miRNA expression can plausibly contribute to recurrence by promoting proliferation, invasion, and metastatic potential.

The pathway-level implications are broad but concrete. The evidence points to miRNAs regulating cell-cycle regulators, proliferation, differentiation, invasion, migration, and cell death [N4-F2]. In thyroid cancer, miR-146b is highlighted as one of the most overexpressed miRNAs and is positively correlated with tumor aggressiveness and extrathyroidal tumor extension [N4-F2]. It is also tied to RARβ, a tumor suppressor, with miR-146b predicted to bind RARβ mRNA and reduce its expression [N4-F2]. This suggests that miRNA upregulation can disrupt pathways that normally constrain tumor growth and metastasis. Similarly, miR-181a and miR-146a differ between cancerous and benign lesions and are reported to vary pre- and post-operatively, indicating they are biologically relevant in thyroid cancer states [N4-R2]. Together, these miRNAs are not just passive markers; they appear to participate in the molecular machinery of tumor progression.

Regarding recurrence versus overall survival, the evidence is mixed. Some studies focus on recurrence-specific outcomes. For example, the review explicitly states that recurrence is a major concern in thyroid cancer because 10–15% of patients show signs of disease recurrence during follow-up, which is associated with shorter overall survival [N4-F2]. This means that miRNA associations with recurrence may overlap with associations with survival, but recurrence itself is a distinct clinical endpoint. The evidence also shows that miRNA-based prognostic models can be developed to track long-term prognosis and recurrence of papillary thyroid cancer [N2-R3]. This indicates that some miRNA studies explicitly model recurrence rather than only overall survival. However, the evidence base here is thinner for direct miRNA-recurrence causality than for miRNA associations with progression biomarkers and survival-related endpoints.

The strongest biological plausibility comes from miRNAs that alter cell survival, migration, or immune evasion. miR-221 and miR-222 are tied to p27 suppression and thus to cell-cycle progression, which supports a role in survival and proliferation rather than recurrence per se [N4-F2]. miR-146b is associated with tumor aggressiveness and extrathyroidal extension, supporting a migration/invasion pathway [N4-F2]. The review also notes that miRNA dysregulation can affect invasion, migration, and cell death [N4-F2]. While immune evasion is not explicitly detailed for every miRNA in the evidence, the broader context of thyroid cancer recurrence includes immune escape as one of the mechanisms contributing to recurrence [N3-F4]. So the miRNA biology supports the plausibility that upregulated miRNAs can promote recurrence by altering cell behavior and tumor microenvironment interactions.

Overall, the evidence supports miRNAs as biologically plausible contributors to thyroid cancer recurrence, but the distinction between general progression, survival, and recurrence-specific biology is important. The strongest direct recurrence plausibility comes from miRNAs linked to tumor aggressiveness, extrathyroidal extension, and migration-related functions, while the broader evidence set also includes miRNAs associated with differentiation and cell-cycle control [N4-R1][N4-F2][N4-R2].

What sensitivity analysis does to miRNA-recurrence relationships

Sensitivity analysis in miRNA-recurrence studies is primarily used to assess whether an association is robust or spurious and to quantify how model assumptions or confounding can alter the observed relationship. The evidence shows that sensitivity analysis in survival prognostic prediction is designed to examine the sensitivity of a multi-gene predictor to dependent censoring, which is a common problem in survival data where censoring is not independent of survival outcomes [N1-F1]. In this context, the analysis is not just a descriptive check; it is a methodological tool for evaluating whether the association between miRNA expression and recurrence is stable under alternative assumptions about data structure and censoring mechanisms [N1-F1].

The statistical assumptions and model choices tested by sensitivity analysis include the independence of censoring, the validity of survival modeling assumptions, and the robustness of gene selection or biomarker selection procedures. The review emphasizes that traditional Cox regression relies on the independent censoring assumption and may fail when survival time and censoring time are dependent, which is common in observational studies [N1-F1]. Sensitivity analysis addresses this by adapting methods such as copula-based gene selection and the copula-graphic estimator to dependent censoring and by implementing them in a way that allows researchers to examine the impact of different dependent censoring mechanisms [N1-F1]. This means sensitivity analysis can test whether a miRNA-recurrence association is preserved when the model accounts for censoring dependence, rather than assuming independence [N1-F1].

The kinds of uncertainty or confounding the analysis addresses are substantial. First, dependent censoring is a major source of bias in survival data, and sensitivity analysis explicitly tests how this affects prognostic prediction [N1-F1]. Second, the evidence from causal mediation analysis shows that sensitivity analysis can be used to examine how estimates of direct and indirect effects change under plausible violations of assumptions, including exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounding [N5-F3]. For miRNA-recurrence relationships, this suggests that sensitivity analysis can separate whether an association is due to a direct effect of the miRNA on recurrence, an indirect effect via another mediator, or confounding by unmeasured variables [N5-F3]. Third, the broader causal inference literature indicates that sensitivity analysis can help assess unmeasured confounding and selection bias by exploring the robustness of estimates under alternative assumptions [N5-F3][N6-R5]. In miRNA studies, this is especially important because expression levels are often measured after diagnosis and treatment, and selection bias can arise from differential follow-up or loss to follow-up [N1-F1].

Taken together, sensitivity analysis clarifies miRNA-recurrence relationships by identifying robust associations that are not driven by censoring dependence or unmeasured confounding, and by testing the assumptions that underlie survival and biomarker models. It also helps distinguish direct biological effects from indirect effects and from spurious associations that arise when model choices or censoring mechanisms are violated [N1-F1][N5-F3].

How recurrence biology shapes interpretation of miRNA results

Recurrence biology fundamentally shapes how miRNA results are interpreted because recurrence is not a single event but a complex process involving disease stage, tumor heterogeneity, treatment response, and the microenvironment. The evidence shows that recurrence is associated with increased mortality and adverse outcomes, and that recurrence risk is currently predicted using clinical tools, often restaging patients after treatment [N3-F4]. In thyroid cancer, recurrence is most commonly observed in cervical lymph nodes and is linked to dormant cancer cells that may later activate [N3-F4]. This means that miRNA results must be interpreted in the context of whether a biomarker reflects early progression, dormancy, or late recurrence, because different biological states may produce different expression patterns [N3-F4].

The recurrence-related endpoints used in studies vary, but they are generally survival-related and recurrence-specific. The evidence explicitly mentions recurrence as an endpoint in thyroid cancer research, with miRNA-based models being developed to track long-term prognosis and recurrence of papillary thyroid cancer [N2-R3]. It also notes that recurrence risk is often predicted using clinical tools that restage patients after treatment, suggesting that studies may use endpoints such as time to recurrence, disease-free survival, or recurrence-free survival rather than only overall survival [N3-F4]. In addition, the systematic appraisal of risk factors in thyroid cancer reports 46 recurrent versus 455 nonrecurrent tumors and identifies 128 new potential biomarkers associated with recurrence, including miRNAs [N3-F4]. This indicates that recurrence biology is often studied through matched recurrence versus nonrecurrence comparisons, which is important because such designs can separate recurrence-associated expression from general disease burden.

Disease stage, tumor heterogeneity, and treatment affect outcomes in important ways. The evidence notes that thyroid cancer recurrence is associated with advanced disease stage, extrathyroidal invasion, lymph node metastasis, and resistance to radioactive iodine therapy [N4-F2][N3-F4]. In the thyroid cancer systematic appraisal, the authors analyze mRNA, microRNA, and somatic mutation data across 46 recurrent and 455 nonrecurrent tumors, and they use functional assays to test the impact of candidate biomarkers on cell migration [N3-F4]. This suggests that heterogeneity across tumor subtypes and recurrence phenotypes is a key concern. The review also emphasizes that recurrence biology includes mechanisms such as increased angiogenesis, escape from immune detection, and changes in the extracellular matrix [N3-F4]. These heterogeneous pathways mean that a miRNA associated with recurrence may be a driver of one pathway but only a bystander in another, and sensitivity analysis is needed to distinguish those roles [N3-F4][N5-F3].

Sensitivity analysis can help distinguish recurrence drivers from bystander effects by testing whether associations are stable under alternative assumptions, including censoring dependence, mediator-outcome confounding, and unmeasured confounding [N1-F1][N5-F3]. In thyroid cancer, recurrence is often studied in observational settings where treatment and follow-up patterns can introduce selection bias [N1-F1]. Sensitivity analysis can therefore assess whether an miRNA-recurrence association persists after accounting for these biases, rather than treating it as a spurious correlation [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Moreover, because recurrence may involve both direct tumor behavior and indirect effects such as immune evasion or dormancy, sensitivity analysis can help separate whether an miRNA is genuinely driving recurrence or merely coinciding with it [N5-F3][N3-F4].

In short, recurrence biology makes miRNA interpretation difficult because recurrence is a multistage, heterogeneous process influenced by disease stage, treatment response, and the tumor microenvironment. Sensitivity analysis helps by testing whether observed associations are robust to model assumptions and by distinguishing true recurrence drivers from confounded or bystander effects [N1-F1][N5-F3][N3-F4].

Causal interpretation and limitations of miRNA-recurrence associations

The evidence indicates that observed miRNA-recurrence associations are often at best correlated, and causal interpretation is limited by observational design, confounding, and the difficulty of separating direct from indirect effects. The causal inference literature in the shared evidence emphasizes that mediation analysis and sensitivity analysis are needed because many mediation effects are not identified when there is exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounding, and because the assumptions underlying causal mediation are often strong [N5-F3]. This directly supports the conclusion that miRNA-recurrence associations cannot be interpreted as direct causal relationships without strong assumptions.

Sensitivity analysis addresses unmeasured confounding and selection bias by testing how estimates change under plausible violations of assumptions. The survival analysis evidence explicitly notes that traditional Cox regression assumes independent censoring, which may be violated when survival time is censored dependently on health status or when patients drop out due to worsening condition [N1-F1]. Sensitivity analysis using copula-based methods and the copula-graphic estimator addresses this by allowing researchers to examine the impact of dependent censoring on prognostic prediction [N1-F1]. Similarly, the causal mediation literature shows that sensitivity analysis can examine the sensitivity of direct and indirect effects to exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounding, which is a major limitation of observational studies [N5-F3]. For miRNA-recurrence associations, this means that sensitivity analysis can assess whether an association is robust to unmeasured confounding and whether the result is sensitive to selection bias in follow-up [N1-F1][N5-F3].

The causal assumptions required for direct/indirect effect separation are substantial and include the assumption of no unmeasured confounding, the assumption that mediator-outcome confounding is not induced by the exposure, and the assumption that the exposure, mediator, and outcome are measured without error [N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that natural direct and indirect effects are not identified if the exposure affects a variable that in turn confounds the mediator-outcome relationship [N5-F3]. This means that causal mediation analysis cannot be applied directly to many observational miRNA-recurrence studies without making strong assumptions that are often untestable. The evidence further indicates that sensitivity analysis is useful precisely because it can examine a range of plausible estimates even when effects are not identified [N5-F3]. For miRNA-recurrence studies, this suggests that researchers should not treat an association as causal unless they can show that the observed effect is robust under alternative assumptions and that confounding is adequately controlled [N5-F3][N1-F1].

The broader causal inference evidence supports the conclusion that miRNA-recurrence associations are likely correlated rather than causal in most observational studies. The evidence on causal survival analysis and causal inference for survival analysis shows that these methods combine survival analysis with causal inference to evaluate treatment or intervention effects, but they still require strong assumptions to move from association to causation [N6-R2][N6-R5]. In thyroid cancer, where recurrence is often studied using clinical and biomarker features rather than randomized trials, causal interpretation is especially limited [N3-F4]. Therefore, the most defensible conclusion is that miRNA-recurrence associations are observational and should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive causal evidence, with sensitivity analysis playing a central role in assessing robustness and addressing confounding [N5-F3][N1-F1][N6-R5].

## Integrated explanation of how sensitivity analysis clarifies miRNA-thyroid cancer recurrence relationships

Sensitivity analysis is a central tool for clarifying whether an association between a specific upregulated miRNA and thyroid cancer recurrence is robust, spurious, or best interpreted as a correlation rather than a direct causal relationship. In the context of miRNA-recurrence studies, it does not simply confirm a statistical association; it tests how sensitive that association is to underlying assumptions, model choices, and sources of uncertainty. The evidence from the branch reports shows that sensitivity analysis addresses dependent censoring, mediator-outcome confounding, and unmeasured confounding, while also helping separate direct effects from indirect effects [N1-F1][N5-F3][N6-R5].

### 1) Sensitivity analysis identifies robust vs. spurious miRNA-recurrence associations

Sensitivity analysis helps distinguish between associations that are likely meaningful and those that may arise from model assumptions or confounding. In survival prognostic prediction, it is explicitly used to examine how much a multi-gene predictor is affected by dependent censoring, which is a common problem in survival data where censoring is not independent of survival outcomes [N1-F1]. For miRNA-recurrence relationships, this means the analysis can reveal whether an observed association holds when the model accounts for censoring dependence, rather than assuming independence [N1-F1].

The causal mediation literature further shows that sensitivity analysis can test whether estimates of direct and indirect effects change under plausible violations of assumptions, including exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounding [N5-F3]. For miRNA-recurrence studies, this is especially important because the association between miRNA expression and recurrence may reflect a direct effect on tumor behavior, an indirect effect through another mediator, or simply a correlated outcome that is not truly causal [N5-F3]. By varying assumptions and observing how the results change, sensitivity analysis can therefore help identify whether an association is robust or spurious [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### 2) Sensitivity analysis tests statistical assumptions and model choices

Sensitivity analysis tests the statistical assumptions that underlie survival and biomarker models. The branch reports show that traditional Cox regression relies on the assumption that survival time and censoring time are independent, but this assumption is often violated in observational studies [N1-F1]. Sensitivity analysis addresses this by using methods such as copula-based gene selection and the copula-graphic estimator, which are explicitly designed to handle dependent censoring and to assess how different censoring mechanisms affect prognostic prediction [N1-F1]. This is directly relevant to miRNA-recurrence studies because miRNA expression is often measured in the context of survival outcomes, and the observed association may be sensitive to how censoring is handled [N1-F1].

In addition, sensitivity analysis can test whether gene selection or biomarker selection procedures are stable under alternative assumptions. The survival prognostic prediction evidence indicates that methods are often evaluated using univariate Cox regression with significance thresholds, cross-validation, and external validation, and that sensitivity analysis can extend this by examining how the model behaves under different censoring assumptions [N1-F1]. For miRNA-recurrence studies, this means that the choice of biomarker set, survival model, and selection criteria can themselves be tested for robustness [N1-F1].

### 3) Sensitivity analysis addresses uncertainty and confounding

Sensitivity analysis addresses several major sources of uncertainty and confounding in miRNA-recurrence studies:

- **Dependent censoring**: In survival data, censoring may depend on health status, follow-up time, or other factors related to the outcome itself [N1-F1]. Sensitivity analysis using copula-based methods is specifically designed to examine how such dependent censoring affects prognostic prediction [N1-F1].
- **Unmeasured confounding**: The causal inference literature shows that sensitivity analysis can be used to assess how estimates change under plausible violations of the assumption that there is no unmeasured confounding [N5-F3][N6-R5]. In miRNA studies, unmeasured confounders could include tumor subtype, treatment history, biomarker expression patterns, or other heterogeneity that is not captured in the model.
- **Selection bias**: Because thyroid cancer recurrence is often studied using observational data, selection bias can arise from differential follow-up, loss to follow-up, or differential treatment assignment [N1-F1]. Sensitivity analysis can assess how robust an association is to these biases [N1-F1].
- **Mediator-outcome confounding**: The causal mediation literature shows that sensitivity analysis can examine exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounding, which can make natural direct and indirect effects unidentifiable [N5-F3]. This is relevant to miRNA-recurrence relationships because an miRNA may influence recurrence through a mediator such as proliferation, migration, or immune evasion, and the observed association may not reflect the true causal pathway [N5-F3].

### 4) Sensitivity analysis helps separate direct from indirect effects

One of the most important ways sensitivity analysis clarifies miRNA-thyroid cancer recurrence relationships is by helping separate direct effects from indirect effects. The branch reports show that mediation analysis is used to break the total effect into direct and indirect components, with the direct effect being the effect of the exposure on the outcome independent of the mediator, and the indirect effect being the effect that operates through the mediator [N5-F3]. For miRNA-recurrence studies, this means that the choice of biomarker set, survival model, and selection criteria can themselves be tested for robustness [N1-F1].
